findings.title: Multi-provider selection is nondeterministic and removes fail-fast FIPS guard
findings.body: This change removes the previous guard that threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found, and instead silently picks the highest-order provider. However DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so the only provider that is actually disambiguated is AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100). If two of the real providers land on the classpath together (e.g. a FIPS deployment that also has the default provider), selection among the equal-order providers falls back to the ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order, which is not guaranteed stable across filesystems/containers. The result is that a non-FIPS provider can be chosen silently in a deployment that previously failed fast at startup, disabling FIPS without any error. FIPS should have a strictly higher order than the non-FIPS providers (or the removed guard should be retained for genuinely conflicting providers).

findings.title: Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public interface in keycloak-common, and order() is added as an abstract method rather than a default method. Every existing implementation (including third-party providers and the keycloak-client code the PR description says will be synced later) must now add this method; old implementations that do not will fail to compile / fail at link time. Making it a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve compatibility while still letting providers opt into precedence.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented/contractually expected to return a BouncyCastle security provider, but this implementation returns the Provider of `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType())` (typically the JDK SUN provider, or whatever the default keystore type resolves to). Any consumer that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BouncyCastle algorithm registration/lookup will get the wrong provider and may fail with NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider or silently use different crypto. All other unsupported methods in this class throw UnsupportedOperationException; this one should do the same unless it genuinely provides a BouncyCastle provider.

findings.title: Dead ASN1Encoder calls whose results are discarded
findings.body: Lines 114-115 build two ASN1Encoder instances (write(rBigInteger) and write(sBigInteger)) and throw the results away; the returned value is produced separately by the chained writeDerSeq(...) call. These two statements have no effect and only allocate objects. They are leftover code and should be removed, since they can mislead a reader into thinking the sequence is built from them.

findings.title: ECDSA round-trip test uses one default-curve key and never verifies the signature
findings.body: The test generates a single `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (default curve, normally P-256) and reuses it for ES256/384/512. It only checks that asn1derToConcatenatedRS -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS is idempotent; it never verifies the produced signature with the public key and never exercises the actual 521-bit curve. Because the padding to `signLength` is symmetric, a wrong per-curve length/endianness/truncation would still round-trip and the test would pass. Generating a key per algorithm's curve and asserting Signature.verify would actually validate curve-specific behavior.

findings.title: New provider-ordering selection logic is not covered by tests
findings.body: detectProvider now sorts multiple providers by order() and ignores the lower-ordered ones, but there is no test that loads multiple CryptoProviders and asserts the highest-order one is selected (or that ties behave sanely). Given this ordering is the central mechanism of the PR, a test using a custom ServiceLoader/classloader with two known-order providers would guard the selection logic against regressions and would have surfaced the equal-order ambiguity noted for the real providers.
